newsitem.title: INDIA: Pakistan ready to "talk and talk" for peace.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan ready to "talk and talk" for peace.

text.p: Striking a note of optimism on the eve of a new round of peace talks, Pakistan's negotiator said on Tuesday that Islamabad was determined to settle differences with India no matter how long it took.

"As long as I am the foreign minister, I will not allow a deadlock to come about," Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told reporters in the Indian capital where he was attending a meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement.
"We will try to resolve it no matter how long it takes. We will talk and talk and talk."

Khan's upbeat comments came hours before he and his Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral were to hold their first face-to-face talks to try to ease half a century of strains which have led to three wars.

The breakfast meeting, set to begin at 9 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Wednesday, was not expected to last more than one and a half hours -- far less than the two days which had been tentatively set aside before a political crisis erupted in New Delhi.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Friday will face a vote of confidence which was triggered 10 days ago when the Congress party withdrew its crucial support.
Congress announced its challenge to Deve Gowda while talks between Indian and Pakistani foreign secretaries -- the first high-level negotiations in three years -- were underway in New Delhi.

"It will be an ice-breaking session, a session where we will get to know each other," Khan said of Wednesday's meeting. "Two days were not possible due to the internal political situation in your country."
In an interview with Cable News Network (CNN) television, Khan played down the impact of the political crisis.

"By and large the foreign policy of India may not undergo a drastic change," Khan said. "We are hopeful whichever government there is, existing or a new government, that we'd continue this dialogue in a fruitful manner."
Bilateral talks broke down in early 1994 over Kashmir, which has been divided between the neighbouring nations since 1947 and was the cause of two of their three wars.
Pakistan had insisted on progress in resolving differences over Kashmir before tackling other issues.
But Khan said Pakistan's new government, headed by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, was keen on "step-by-step, confidence building measures" before getting to the main issues.
"From Pakistan's point of view, the core issue is Kashmir and as I have suggested, that can be dealt with in a step-by-step manner and a lot can be solved," he said.

The Pakistani negotiator told CNN that as a start, India could reduce the number of security forces in Jammu and Kashmir state, where more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.

Khan said the economies of India and Pakistan would stand to benefit from a thaw in tension. He cited greater trade, a pipeline from Turkmenistan and electricity from Pakistan to power-starved northern India. "The countries of northeast Asia which used to make baskets out of bamboo sticks and were involved in wood crafts -- look to where they have progressed today. And where are India and Pakistan today?" he said.
"It is all because we are spending all our money on mutual fighting. In 50 years we have ended up fighting three times. Who gained from this? Neither India nor Pakistan."
